messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Frank has been driving a city bus for twenty-seven years, and for twenty-six of them, he loved it. He knew the rhythm of the streets, the faces of the regulars, the particular sigh the air brakes made at the end of a long day. But for the last eight months, the driver’s seat has felt like a cage. It all started on a Tuesday night in late autumn. He was driving his own car home after a double shift, the kind of bone-deep tired that makes your eyelids feel like lead weights. He pulled over onto the gravel shoulder of a quiet access road, just for a moment, to close his eyes. The sudden crunch of footsteps and the wrenching open of his passenger door happened so fast he barely had time to register it. The man who forced his way in smelled of stale cigarettes and something metallic. What followed has since become a film that plays in Frank’s mind on a relentless loop, unspooling without his permission. He remembers the click of the door lock, the rough fabric of the man’s jacket against his cheek, and the feeling of utter, paralyzing powerlessness.

Now, that film reel can be started by almost anything. Driving his route, a job that once felt like second nature, has become a minefield. The hiss of the doors opening to let on a passenger can be enough to make his heart hammer against his ribs. He finds himself watching the rearview mirror not for traffic, but for faces, scanning each one for a flicker of threat. He has come to believe, with a certainty that feels absolute, that people simply can't be trusted. The easy chatter he used to have with his regulars has evaporated; now, a passenger standing too close to his seat can send a jolt of ice through his veins. When the memory hits him on the bus, the terror is as fresh and sharp as it was that night in his car. It’s a full-body experience: the cold sweat, the tightening in his chest, the desperate urge to flee his own vehicle. He grips the wheel until his knuckles are white, focusing on the yellow line on the road, praying he doesn't swerve.

Following the terror, a wave of profound shame always washes over him. It’s a hot, sticky feeling that starts in his gut and spreads through his limbs. When he remembers the event, he feels an intense disgust for his own body, a sense that it was defiled and that he somehow failed to protect it. He can’t look at himself in the mirror for long anymore and flinches when his wife, Maria, reaches for him in bed. He hasn’t been able to explain to her why. The words get stuck in his throat, choked by the conviction that what happened to his body is too humiliating to speak aloud.

The most difficult trigger is the most mundane: exhaustion. The very feeling that led him to pull over that night now serves as a potent internal alarm. As his shift wears on and fatigue sets in, the memories become more vivid, more intrusive. The film plays with greater clarity. He has started refusing overtime, and twice in the last month, he has called in sick because the thought of driving while tired was unbearable. His supervisor has noticed the change, commenting on his recent unreliability. Frank used to be a man of faith, a quiet churchgoer, but that has been lost, too. He feels adrift in a world that no longer seems to have any inherent goodness or safety.

He decided to seek help after an incident last week. A teenager boarded his bus with a loud group of friends, and the sound of their boisterous laughter and the rustle of their jackets as they jostled past him sent him spiraling. For a full thirty seconds, he wasn't on Main Street; he was back on that dark road, the same terror constricting his throat. He missed a stop, and a passenger shouted at him. The complaint, he knows, is now in his file. The fear of losing his job—the one piece of his old life he has clung to—was finally greater than the shame of speaking about what happened. He is here now because he doesn’t know how else to stop the film from playing, terrified that one day it will start and he won’t be able to make it stop at all.
